vignette:
She is thirty-four years old, a prison guard at a maximum-security facility in a Midwestern city, and every morning she puts on the stiff navy uniform like she is suiting up for battle. The weight of the badge against her chest feels both absurd and necessary-absurd because she knows what it means to be on the other side of steel doors, necessary because if she can control the locked-down order here, maybe she can keep the chaos inside her head at bay. It never works.

Her story begins fifteen years ago, in a small town in Central America where she was still a girl. She remembers the night the house fell quiet-no birds, no dogs, just the low hum of motorcycles. Her father had been a union organizer. The men came with machetes and a list. She hid under the bed with her younger brother, her hand clamped over his mouth, her own breath so shallow she thought she would die from the holding. They found her father in the yard. She heard the wet thuds, then the dragging. Then silence. Her mother grabbed them through the back door, and they ran into the dark without shoes.

That night became a tunnel she has never fully exited. The border crossing came later-coyotes, a truck that smelled of diesel and sweat, a river where she nearly lost her brother. When they finally reached the United States, she was hollowed out, a shell that ate and walked and learned English, but never stopped listening for motorcycles.

Now she works in a place where doors lock from the outside. She chose this job because it pays well and because, she tells herself, she can handle the tough men inside. But every clang of a cell gate sends her heart into a sideways gallop. The crackle of the radio makes her freeze mid-step. She has learned to hide it-she stands tall, eyes hard, voice flat-but her colleagues have noticed the way she flinches when an inmate shouts, the way she sometimes stares at the floor as if it might open up. They call her "hard," "professional," "scary." She does not correct them.

At home, her husband, a mild-mannered mechanic, tries to reach her. He says she is not there. He is right. She sleeps in fits, jerking awake at 3 a.m. with the smell of diesel in her nose and the image of her mother's hand slipping away in the dark. She avoids crowded places-the grocery store on Saturdays, family barbecues, even the church where she once found comfort. She tells herself she just does not like people. But what she really cannot stand is the feeling of being trapped in a line, or the sound of a man raising his voice, or the sight of a uniformed officer-even herself-because uniforms remind her of the men who stood guard at the border checkpoint, the men who made her mother beg.

She has become a guard who flinches at her own reflection.

The worst part is the rage. It bubbles up without warning-a flash of white-hot fury when an inmate refuses an order, or when her husband asks one too many questions about her day. She once slammed a file cabinet so hard the handle broke, and later could not explain why. In the evenings, she sits on the back porch with a can of beer, watching the fence line of her small suburban yard, and knows she is doing it again-scanning, listening, waiting-as if the men with machetes might step through the gate.

She came to therapy because her husband said he was leaving if she did not. She sat in the chair with her arms crossed, uniform still on, and said, "I don't know what you want me to say." But her hands were shaking. She could not look at the door. She could not stop looking at the door.
